opus-5.5.text:
I think about this a lot, because the two pull in different directions. For me, the thing I enjoy most and probably do best is sitting down and writing the code myself. Most of my papers start with me poking at something: running an attack, seeing a weird number, and pulling on that thread. If I stopped doing that entirely and only advised, I think I'd lose the intuition that makes the advice useful in the first place.

So I try to protect a decent amount of time for hands-on work. Usually that means one or two projects where I'm actually driving: writing the experiments, writing the paper, making the calls about what's interesting.

At the same time, a lot of the highest-leverage thing I can do is help someone else avoid wasting three months. Often a short conversation does that. Someone says, "I'm trying to do X," and I can say, "I tried something like that, here's where it breaks," or "That evaluation won't convince anyone, here's what would." That costs me thirty minutes and can save them a huge amount of time. Those conversations I almost always say yes to.

Where I'm more careful is the middle ground: being nominally on a project without really contributing. I don't think that's good for anyone. Either I'm in, and I'm actually running experiments or writing sections, or I'm out and happy to give feedback whenever asked. I try hard not to be the person whose name is on the paper but who only showed up for the final read.

A big part of it is also just being honest about what I'm good at. I'm not the best manager of large teams. I'm reasonably good at quickly figuring out whether an idea is going to work. So I lean into the kind of help that uses that, quick sanity checks and "here's how I'd break this," and leave longer-term mentorship to people who are better at it than I am.

r001.rationale: The response describes advice that can save collaborators time, but it does not mention PhD students or compare that help with personally doing low-level GPU implementation.

r002.rationale: It says he protects a “decent amount of time” for hands-on work and drives one or two projects, but does not state that this is at least half his time.

r003.rationale: It connects his technical involvement to the papers he drives, but does not explain how his sense of which papers are his own relates to his total publication count.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I don't really try to balance it in any principled way, and I'm probably bad at it. But let me try to describe what actually happens.

The thing I care about most is being the person who actually does the work. I write the code for basically all of my papers. I think this is really important, and I'd push back on the idea that it's something you grow out of. The reason is that most of the interesting things I've found came from being hands-on with the system. You run the attack, it doesn't work, and you have to figure out why. And the "why" is usually the actual contribution. If you're one level removed from that, if you're just reading plots someone else made, you miss all of the weird little things that don't make it into the plot. So for me, driving the technical work isn't something that competes with doing good research. It is the research.

On the helping-other-people side, I spend a lot of time on it, but I try to be deliberate about what kind of help. The thing I'm most useful for is usually not the idea. People have plenty of ideas. What I can do is say, "I tried this four years ago, here is the specific reason it failed," or, "your evaluation is broken because of this one thing, and here is the sanity check that would have caught it." That kind of feedback takes me twenty minutes and can save someone six months. That is a really good trade, and I'm happy to make it a lot.

What I try not to do is take over. If I start writing the code for someone else's project, I'm now not working on my own stuff, and also I've probably taken the most fun part away from them. So the rule I try to follow, imperfectly, is that I'll tell you what I think is wrong and why, and then it's yours.

I'll also say I think there's a selfish benefit to helping people, which is that it's how I find out what's actually hard. If five different people come to me with the same broken evaluation, that's a signal that maybe I should go write the paper that explains how to do that properly. A lot of my more "service"-type work, the "here's how to evaluate this correctly" papers, came out of exactly that.

So I guess the short version is: I don't balance it so much as I keep the technical work as the thing I protect, and I let the helping be interrupt-driven. When those conflict, which they do, I usually feel guilty for a bit and then go back to writing code.

r001.rationale: The response discusses giving researchers evaluation feedback, but does not identify sharing accumulated judgment with PhD students as a higher-leverage use of time than personally doing low-level GPU implementation.

r002.rationale: It says technical work is something he protects, but gives no claim that he spends at least half his time on papers he personally drives.

r003.rationale: The response emphasizes hands-on technical work, but does not say that which papers he considers his own depends on that involvement rather than his publication count.

astra-6.text:
I think the balance is that I want to be useful to the people I’m working with, but I also want to stay close enough to the technical work that I can actually tell whether my advice is any good. There’s a big difference between having an opinion about an experiment and sitting down, running it, and understanding why it didn’t work.

Sometimes the most useful thing I can do is help someone sharpen a question or figure out what evidence would make the result convincing. Other times, it’s to write code and work through the problem with them. I don’t think every collaboration needs the same division of labor.

But I do want to keep doing things myself. Partly because that’s the part I enjoy, and partly because that’s where a lot of the ideas come from. If you get too far away from the details, it becomes easy to suggest things that sound reasonable but don’t actually make sense once you try them.

r003.rationale: It values direct technical involvement, but does not define which papers feel like his own or contrast that with publication count.

sol-6.1.text:
I really like doing the technical work myself. That’s a big part of why I do research—I enjoy writing the code, running the experiments, and figuring out why something doesn’t work. So I try to be careful about taking on so many collaborations that my entire job becomes giving advice in meetings.

At the same time, helping someone else can be incredibly rewarding. Sometimes they’re stuck on something where a little bit of experience can save them a lot of time. The balance I try to strike is to be useful without taking over. If it’s their project, I want them to have the space to make the decisions and develop their own intuition. And then I want to keep enough time where I’m the person actually wrestling with the problem, because that’s how I keep learning, too.

r001.rationale: The response says experience can help someone get unstuck, but it does not mention PhD students or compare that help with personally doing low-level GPU implementation.

r002.rationale: The response says he wants to preserve time for hands-on work, but gives no half-time target or equivalent proportion.

r003.rationale: The response distinguishes helping with someone else’s project from personally wrestling with a problem, but does not explain how he identifies his own papers or contrast technical involvement with publication count.
